title: Trump Secures G7 Accord for Massive Fuel Release as High Diesel Prices Sting Americans Ahead of Midterms
snippet: Facing intense political pressure from soaring fuel costs, President Donald Trump announced a G7 deal to release 100 million barrels of crude and refined products—starting immediately with a major injection of diesel.
content:
WASHINGTON — Under rising political pressure over soaring fuel costs just weeks before the November midterm elections, President Donald Trump announced Friday that the U.S. and its G7 allies have agreed to inject 100 million barrels of oil and refined products into the global market.

The move kicks off with an immediate, frontloaded deployment of diesel designed to cool skyrocketing prices that have hammered American truckers and consumers alike. The initial wave of diesel will roll out over the next 20 days, with the remainder of the energy stockpile released over a four-month period.

Relief at the Pump Ahead of November

The announcement arrives as President Trump faces mounting scrutiny over his economic stewardship. An ongoing war with Iran and escalating foreign trade disputes have pushed domestic energy prices to historic highs. On Friday, the national average for a gallon of diesel stood at $6.37, down slightly from a record peak of $6.52 set late last month, according to AAA data.

With Trump embarking on a aggressive campaign swing to protect Republican majorities in Congress, energy experts suggest the emergency release could offer tangible relief within weeks. Analysts estimate the influx of European diesel reserves could lower U.S. pump prices by 25 to 50 cents per gallon by reducing international demand for American exports.

Export Bans Off the Table

Despite calls from several Capitol Hill Republicans urging the administration to halt U.S. diesel exports to protect domestic supply, Trump firmly rejected the idea following virtual talks led by French President Emmanuel Macron.

"We’re not going to be doing the export ban," Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday, emphasizing that G7 partners agreed not to restrict energy trade among member nations. "We’re going to be doing what we’re supposed to do. Europe is making a major world contribution, and so are we."

Energy analysts had warned that a domestic export ban could backfire by forcing refiners to curtail overall operations, inadvertently squeezing gasoline supplies.

Global Shocks and Long-Term Risks

Global diesel supplies have taken severe hits from multiple fronts, including Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries, Moscow's subsequent export bans, and war-related supply disruptions in the Persian Gulf. While the coordinated release triggered a 2% drop in crude prices on Friday, energy policy experts caution that draining strategic reserves carries significant long-term risks.

With active conflicts continuing to threaten global energy infrastructure, depleting emergency stockpiles now could leave Western nations vulnerable if prices surge again later. Nevertheless, administration officials are banking on the emergency injection to stabilize volatile markets and provide immediate relief to American voters.
